passages.happening:
Joshua calls together the men of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. They had crossed the Jordan in chapter 1 to fight beside the other tribes, leaving their families on the east side. Now he releases them.

“You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice in all that I commanded you. All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day” (verses 2-3). The LORD has given the other tribes rest, as he promised. They may go home (verse 4).

He gives them one charge to carry with them: “But be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you: to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (verse 5).

He sends them off with his good wishes and with great wealth in herds, metals and clothing, and tells them to share it with those who stayed at home (verse 8). They leave Shiloh for Gilead (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
A promise made in the first chapter is kept in the twenty-second. These tribes had their land before anyone else. They could have stayed on it. They had given Moses their word that they would cross and fight until their brothers had land too, and they did. The wars lasted for years. All that time their own fields and families were on the other side of the river.

Joshua says so in front of everyone: ‘you have not deserted your brothers’. The book lets these men hear that they did well.

Then he tells them what to take home. It is not a list of rules. It is five verbs: love, walk, keep, hold fast, serve. The words are the words of Deuteronomy. Everything Moses asked of Israel is gathered into a few lines for men about to live a long way from the sanctuary.

That distance is the point of the charge. Shiloh, with the tent of God's presence, is in the hills west of the Jordan. These tribes are going to live beyond a deep river valley, nearer to other peoples and other gods. Joshua cannot go with them. What he can give them is this: hold fast.

The order to share the spoil with those who stayed behind follows an old rule in Israel. The people who guarded the homes had a part in the reward with the people who fought.
passages.later:
The charge Joshua gives is Moses' own summary of what God asks: “And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 10:12).

King David later made the sharing of spoil a fixed rule: “The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike” (1 Samuel 30:24).
passages.asks: These men kept a costly promise for years, and Joshua told them so in public. Ask who has stood by you through a long, hard stretch and has never heard you say it. Then take Joshua's five verbs one at a time: love, walk, keep, hold fast, serve. Ask which of them is weakest in you now, and what holding fast would look like where you live, at a distance from the people who first taught you.

passages.t: An altar by the river, and an army gathered
passages.happening:
On their way home the eastern tribes stop beside the Jordan and build ‘an imposing altar’ (verse 10).

Word reaches the others, and their answer is immediate. “And when they heard this, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them” (verse 12).

Before they march, they send a delegation: Phinehas, the son of Eleazar the priest, and ten chiefs, one from each of the western tribes (verses 13-14).

The delegation speaks sharply. “What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD and building for yourselves an altar, that you might rebel against the LORD this day?” (verse 16). They bring up two old disasters, the sin at Peor and the sin of Achan, when one group's wrong brought suffering on everyone (verses 17, 20).

And they make an offer. If the land east of the river seems unclean to them, they should cross over and take land among the other tribes, near the LORD's tabernacle. “But do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
To see why an altar could bring Israel to the edge of civil war, a reader needs one law in mind. Moses had commanded that Israel bring its sacrifices only to the one place God would choose, and not set up altars wherever it liked. One altar meant one God and one people. A second altar, and a large one, looked like a rival sanctuary. It looked like the first step toward another religion.

The western tribes also had reason to be afraid. At Peor, in the wilderness, some Israelites had joined in the worship of another god, and a plague had killed thousands. At Jericho, Achan had taken what was devoted to God, and men had died at Ai. Both times the whole people suffered for what a part of it did. These tribes had learned at great cost that sin in one corner of Israel was everyone's concern.

So their alarm was not foolish, and their care for God's honor was real. But notice the order of events. They hear a report. They gather for war. Only then do they send someone to ask. They have reached a verdict before they have heard a word from the accused. Their speech is not a question. It is a charge. They say ‘breach of faith’, the very word used of Achan. They say ‘rebel’ again and again.

Two things in their favor should be seen. First, they did send. An army stood ready, and they held it back long enough to talk. Second, their offer in verse 19 is generous. They say, in effect, that if the problem is the land, the eastern tribes can come and share theirs. They are willing to give up their own ground to keep their brothers. People who only wanted a fight would not have said that.

The man they send to lead the delegation is Phinehas. At Peor he had acted with a spear. Here the same man goes to ask and to listen.
passages.later:
Moses' law about the one place of sacrifice reads, “Be careful not to offer your burnt offerings in just any place you see; you must offer them only in the place the LORD will choose in one of your tribal territories” (Deuteronomy 12:13-14).

A proverb describes the danger the western tribes came close to: “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17).

Jesus gave his followers a rule for the moment when one believes another has done wrong. It begins with a conversation: “If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over” (Matthew 18:15).
passages.asks: The western tribes heard a report and gathered an army before they had asked one question. Ask whom you have already judged on the strength of what you heard about them. Ask what you would need to do to hear it from them. And notice the offer in verse 19. Ask whether you care enough about anyone you disagree with to give up something of your own to keep them.

passages.happening:
The eastern tribes answer with an oath. “The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! He knows, and may Israel also know. If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today” (verse 22).

Then they explain. They built the altar out of fear for their children. One day the children of the western tribes might say to theirs, ‘What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?’ (verse 24). The Jordan would be called a border, and their children would be told, ‘You have no share in the LORD’ (verse 25).

So they built an altar that was never meant for sacrifice. It is ‘a witness between us and you and the generations to come’ (verse 27). If anyone ever says their children do not belong, they can point to it: a copy of the LORD's altar, made by their fathers, ‘not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you’ (verse 28).

Phinehas and the chiefs hear this and are satisfied. Phinehas says, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him” (verse 31). They carry the report home. The Israelites are glad, praise God, ‘and spoke no more about going to war against them’ (verse 33).

The eastern tribes name the altar Witness: “It is a witness between us that the LORD is God” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The accused tribes do not answer anger with anger. They begin with God's name, said twice, and with an oath that puts their own lives at stake if they are lying. Then they tell the truth about what they were afraid of.

Their fear was reasonable. The Jordan runs in a deep valley, and the land east of it was another world, far from Shiloh. In a few generations people might well forget that the families beyond the river were part of the same people. The altar was built to guard against being shut out.

So the two sides had been afraid of the same thing from opposite directions. The western tribes feared that the easterners were leaving the LORD. The eastern tribes feared that they would be told they had no part in him. The object that looked like rebellion was a plea to belong.

The word that changes everything is ‘witness’. In Hebrew a witness can be a thing as well as a person, such as a stone or a heap set up to testify to an agreement. The altar is a copy. It says to anyone who sees it that the people on this side worship at the one altar on the other.

It must be said that the eastern tribes could have spared everyone a great deal by explaining before they built. A large altar with no word of explanation was bound to be misread. The story has no party without fault and no villain.

And it ends well for one reason. Someone asked, and someone listened. Phinehas and the chiefs came ready for the worst. When they heard a good answer they accepted it. They did not hunt for a reason to stay angry or to save face. The same men who had brought the charge carried home the news that there was nothing in it.

The Hebrew of the last verse does not plainly give the altar a name. Translations supply the word ‘Witness’ from the sense of the sentence.
passages.later:
The book of Judges tells of a time when a quarrel inside Israel was not settled this way. A demand was sent to the tribe of Benjamin, “But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites” (Judges 20:13). A civil war followed, and a tribe was almost wiped out.

James gives the rule the delegation followed in the end: “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

Paul writes of a deeper division healed in Christ, who ‘has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility’ (Ephesians 2:14).
passages.hard:
Were the western tribes wrong to gather for war before they knew the facts?

They did assemble for war first (verse 12). But they did not march. They sent priests and leaders to ask, and they accepted the answer.

Readers see the chapter in two ways. Some see it as praising the western tribes' zeal for God's honor, given what Peor and Achan had cost. Others see a warning about how fast suspicion turns toward violence, and they note that a civil war in the book of Judges did go ahead.

Many hold the two together. The chapter honors care for the true worship of God. And it shows that what kept that care from ending in bloodshed was the willingness to ask and to listen.

Nothing in the chapter supports the use of force over a disagreement about worship. What it holds up is the conversation that made force unnecessary.
passages.asks: Both sides were afraid of the same loss, and neither knew it until they talked. Ask whether a conflict you are in might look different if you heard what the other person is afraid of. If you are the one who built the ‘altar’, ask what you could have explained beforehand. And if you came ready to accuse and heard a good answer, ask whether you are able to be glad about it, as Phinehas was.
